title: Europe's most active volcano might be one of a kind—here's why
summary: Mount Etna is a huge volcano on the island of Sicily in Italy. It's the most active volcano in all of Europe, erupting several times a year! But for a long time, scientists couldn't figure out how it formed. Most volcanoes fit into three neat categories: some form where tectonic plates pull apart, some where one plate dives under another, and some over hot spots deep in the Earth. Etna doesn't match any of those. Now, researchers from the University of Lausanne in Switzerland think they've cracked the puzzle. They say Etna might be a super rare type of volcano called a "petit-spot" volcano. These are usually tiny underwater volcanoes that form when small pockets of magma already sitting in the Earth's upper mantle get squeezed up to the surface. Imagine a wet sponge—when you press it, water comes out. Something similar happens under Sicily: as the African and Eurasian tectonic plates collide, they squeeze little blobs of magma about 50 miles underground, forcing them upward through cracks. That magma feeds Etna's frequent eruptions. What's wild is that petit-spot volcanoes were only discovered in 2006, and they were thought to be small—just a few hundred feet tall. But Mount Etna towers over 9,800 feet! If the scientists are right, Etna is the first giant petit-spot volcano ever found. To test their idea, the team studied lava rocks from Etna that are up to 500,000 years old. They found that the lava's chemistry has stayed almost the same over all that time, which fits the squeezed-sponge model. This discovery could change how geologists think about volcanoes everywhere. Maybe there are other hidden giants waiting to be found.
why_it_matters: Understanding what makes Mount Etna erupt helps scientists warn people living nearby, so families and schools can stay safe when the volcano wakes up.

background_read: Mount Etna is one of the most famous volcanoes on Earth and has been erupting since ancient times—people were writing about it over 2,500 years ago.
Sicily, an Italian island in the Mediterranean Sea, sits right where the African and Eurasian tectonic plates crash into each other very slowly.
If Etna really is a giant petit-spot volcano, it would be the first one ever found that is this big, changing how scientists think volcanoes can grow.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers from the University of Lausanne in Switzerland
WHAT: They think Mount Etna is a super-rare “petit-spot” volcano, formed when colliding plates squeeze pockets of magma upward instead of melting rock deep below
WHERE: Mount Etna, on the island of Sicily, Italy
WHY: To finally solve the mystery of how Europe’s most active volcano formed, and to search for other hidden giant volcanoes around the world

perspectives.description: Finding a giant petit-spot volcano on land is thrilling. It means Earth still has surprises, and we might have to update science textbooks about how mountains form.
Not all scientists agree yet. They want to see more proof and check other big volcanoes before deciding Etna really is a petit-spot type.
For people living near Mount Etna, the volcano is a part of everyday life. It can be dangerous, but the ash also makes the soil very good for farming.
A kid might wonder if there are similar volcanoes on other planets. If magma can be squeezed up here, maybe tiny earthquakes push up lava on Mars or the Moon too.
